source.title_on_document: Two-Player Alternate Uses Test: A Controlled Testbed for Interactive Human–AI and Human–Human Co-Creation

supplement.where: No supplement or online appendix is mentioned. The paper links source code and a live demo (p. 2): https://github.com/BabakHemmatian/AI-creativity and https://co-creativity.onrender.com/. Utility ratings are 'available on request' (p. 4, Sec. 3.4).
supplement.holds: Nothing referenced. Full LMM output tables, arm-level SDs, and the utility results are not in the PDF.

paper_design_summary: Sixty-two UIUC students each completed three 4-minute Alternate Uses Test co-creation sessions in randomized order: with a live human partner (HUM), with a GPT-4 chat partner (GPT), and a non-interactive session reading one of three pre-rated seed sets (CON; GPT-4-only ideas, highly creative human ideas, or uncreative human ideas, assigned between participants). After each session participants curated their best uses, and crowdsourced Prolific workers rated the ideas' originality on a 5-point scale; the analysis uses a linear mixed model with subject, item-within-subject, and rater random intercepts.

studies.label: In-person pilot: two-player AUT with human, GPT-4, and non-interactive partners

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of three partner conditions (HUM, GPT, CON) within person; between participants, which of three seed sets the CON session used (randomization of seed-set assignment not stated); half of participants did the 2-minute solo AUT before the sessions and half after (how split not stated).
assignment.quote: Each participant completed three co-creation sessions within-subject in randomized order: human–human (HUM), human–GPT-4 (GPT), and non-interactive (CON for “constant”).
assignment.locator: p. 3, Sec. 3.2 Experimental Design; Figure 1 (p. 3): 'The CON arm draws one of three pre-rated seed sets, assigned between participants.'
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 5 mentions a confirmatory test 'currently in progress' in a larger sample; no preregistration of this pilot is stated.

arms.name: GPT
arms.description: 4-minute shared-chat AUT co-creation with GPT-4 (OpenAI API, strict turn-taking, one idea per turn), then curate best uses in a survey tab. Every participant does this session. Fig. 3 subgroup counts: n = 32 (low BAS Drive) and n = 29 (high BAS Drive).

arms.name: HUM
arms.description: 4-minute shared-chat AUT co-creation with another participant (two people in shared chat), same interface and instructions. Every participant does this session. Fig. 3 subgroup counts: n = 32 and n = 30.

arms.name: CON
arms.description: Non-interactive session: participant reads one of three pre-rated sets of 16 ideas (no live partner), then curates best uses. Every participant does this session. Fig. 3 subgroup counts: n = 32 and n = 30.

arms.name: CON sub-arm gpt_con
arms.description: CON seed set of 16 GPT-4-only ideas generated by the GPT-4 backend, no external rating. Fig. 1 shows n = 21; text says sub-arms were 'unevenly assigned'.

arms.name: CON sub-arm high_con
arms.description: CON seed set of 16 highly creative human ideas from Stevenson et al. 2022 (both raters scored 4 or 5). Fig. 1 shows n = 21.

arms.name: CON sub-arm low_con
arms.description: CON seed set of 16 uncreative human ideas from Stevenson et al. 2022 (both raters scored 1 or 2). Fig. 1 shows n = 21.

participants.exclusions: None stated. Abstract and Fig. 1 give N = 62. Fig. 3 subgroup counts sum to 62 for CON and HUM but 61 for GPT (32 + 29), so one participant appears to be missing from the GPT subgroup analysis without explanation. Fig. 1 shows n = 21 in each of three CON seed sets (63 in total), which does not match N = 62.
participants.who: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign students who took part for course credit (19 male, 42 female, 1 non-binary), in in-person sessions.
participants.country: United States (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; country not stated explicitly)
participants.quote: Sixty-two University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign students signed up for in-person sessions in exchange for course credit (19 male, 42 female, 1 non-binary).
participants.locator: p. 3, Sec. 3.2; abstract p. 1 ('An in-person pilot (N = 62)'); Figure 1 caption p. 3-4 ('Each participant (N = 62)')

ai_tool.name_model: gpt-4 via OpenAI chat-completions API, temperature 0.7, max_tokens 3000
ai_tool.how_used: Interactive chat partner in a shared chat interface with server-enforced strict turn-taking; the prompt asked for one idea per turn, no preambles, single-sentence responses; a token-overlap filter rejected responses overlapping >50% with prior messages. Participants knew the partner was an AI. In the CON condition, one seed set (gpt_con) consisted of GPT-4-generated ideas shown non-interactively (ideas supplied).

task.description: Two-player Alternate Uses Test: generate unusual uses for a target object (book, fork, tin can; counterbalanced across sessions) together with a partner in a chat, then curate the 'best' uses (Fig. 1: 'best 5') inspired by the chat in a separate survey tab. A 2-minute solo AUT served as a personal baseline (half before, half after the sessions).
task.duration: 4-minute chat per session, three sessions; 2-minute solo AUT

outcomes.name: Originality of ideas, GPT-4 partner vs human partner (interactive sessions)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Crowdsourced originality ('how unlikely others would be to generate the idea'), 5-point Likert, 226 Prolific workers (Fig. 1 says 225), median 6 ratings per idea (range 5-12). Rater modeled as crossed random intercept. LMM with fixed effects of partner type, non-interactive assignment, and their interaction, random intercepts for subject, item-within-subject, and rater. Equivalence also tested by TOST and Bayesian re-estimation (Normal(0,1) prior). Utility was also rated but not reported (available on request).

contrasts.reported: β_{GPT−HUM} = −0.11, SE = 0.13, 95% CI [−0.37, +0.16], p = .42. TOST bounded the maximum credible effect at |β| ≤ 0.33. Bayesian: BF01 = 10.95; posterior median +0.06, 95% credible interval [−0.06, +0.20]. By BAS Drive group (Fig. 3, subject-level means, Welch t-tests): low Drive GPT 3.20 (n = 32) vs HUM 3.10 (n = 32), p = 0.32; high Drive GPT 3.48 (n = 29) vs HUM 3.29 (n = 30), p = 0.08.
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Sec. 4.1 Baseline Originality Across Partner Types; p. 6, Figure 3

outcomes.name: Originality of ideas, GPT-4 partner vs non-interactive seed exposure, moderated by BAS Drive
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same crowdsourced 5-point originality ratings as S1-O1. Interaction term from the mixed model; subgroup comparisons in Fig. 3 are Welch t-tests on subject-level mean originality, split at median BAS Drive = 14.0. The paper reports that the same direction replicates on top-quality rate (p = .033) and failure rate (p = .030), treated here as robustness variants. No main GPT-vs-CON effect is printed.

contrasts.control_arm: CON (pooled over the three seed sets: GPT-4-only, highly creative human, uncreative human ideas)
contrasts.reported: Interaction β_{BAS-Drive × GPT-vs-CON} = +0.20, 95% CI [+0.05, +0.38], p = .034, BF10 = 3.37. Fig. 3: high BAS Drive, CON 3.24 (n = 30) vs GPT 3.48 (n = 29), 'CON vs GPT: Δ = +0.25, p = 0.046*, d = +0.53'; low BAS Drive, CON 3.44 (n = 32) vs GPT 3.20 (n = 32), CON vs GPT p = 0.06.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Sec. 4.2 Participant trait predictors; p. 6, Figure 3

outcomes.name: Originality of CON-session ideas by seed set (GPT-4-only seeds vs human seed sets)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Crowdsourced 5-point originality ratings of 'CON-session ideas', presented as a manipulation check of the seed-set quality gradient. The text does not make clear whether the rated ideas are participants' curated ideas after reading the seeds or the seed ideas themselves (see open_questions). Assignment of seed sets is between participants; randomization of that assignment is not stated.

contrasts.locator: p. 3, Sec. 3.2 Non-interactive baselines; p. 4, Sec. 4.1
p. 3, Sec. 3.2 Non-interactive baselines; p. 4, Sec. 4.1

outcomes.name: Originality in later interactive (HUM and GPT) sessions by initial CON seed set ('seeding' effect)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Crowdsourced 5-point originality ratings of ideas from HUM and GPT sessions, restricted to participants whose first session was CON. The manipulated factor is prior exposure to GPT-4-generated vs human seed ideas; the scored output comes from later sessions where the seed set is no longer shown, pooled over a session with a GPT-4 partner and a session with a human partner. Reported as exploratory because CON sub-arms were unevenly assigned.
outcomes.delay: Later sessions in the same visit; no delay in days.

contrasts.reported: Seed-set effect F(2, 1963) = 4.68, p = .009; β_{high vs gpt} = +0.32, p = .016 (higher originality after highly creative human seeds than after GPT-4 seeds).

company_involvement.description: No AI-developer involvement stated. GPT-4 accessed through the OpenAI API. One author lists the affiliation 'Alinea' (p. 1); no funding or company role is described.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1 affiliations; p. 3 Sec. 3.1 AI configuration

eligibility.reason: Within-person design with randomized order of a GPT-4 chat partner session, a human-partner session, and a non-interactive session (p. 3); 62 students analyzed (abstract, Fig. 1), above 50 but close; Fig. 3 shows 61 in the GPT condition. Outcome is crowdsourced originality ratings of participants' ideas (p. 4). Caveats: pilot study; human-partner arm pairs participants with each other; the comparison to GPT is a human partner (ai_vs_active), not a no-aid arm; scored ideas were curated after the chat in a separate survey tab.

one_line_finding: Originality of AUT ideas with a GPT-4 chat partner did not differ from that with a human partner (β_{GPT−HUM} = −0.11, SE = 0.13, 95% CI [−0.37, +0.16], p = .42; BF01 = 10.95; p. 4, Sec. 4.1), with BAS Drive moderating GPT vs non-interactive exposure (p. 5, Fig. 3 p. 6).
open_questions: Whether the scored ideas are only participants' curated uses or also include ideas typed in the chat, and whether the GPT-4 partner's own ideas are among the 1,923 rated ideas. Fig. 1 says '1,928 ideas ... generated in chat + curated'; 1,928 over 62 × 3 sessions exceeds the 'best 5' curation per session.

S1-O3: whether the manipulation-check ratings (β_{low−gpt} = −0.48, β_{high−gpt} = +0.23) are ratings of participants' CON-session ideas or of the seed ideas themselves. If the latter, the outcome is an AI-vs-human comparison of seed content (question none, ai_vs_human) rather than a participant outcome.
S1-O4: question coding. The AI seed exposure ended before the scored output, but half the scored output comes from sessions with a GPT-4 partner, so availability is mixed; coded after_ai here.
Whether assignment of the CON seed set was random; the paper says only 'assigned between participants' and 'unevenly assigned'.
Inconsistent counts in the document: 1,923 rated ideas (pp. 4, 7) vs 1,928 ideas (pp. 2, 3); 226 raters (p. 4) vs 225 (Fig. 1); three seed sets of n = 21 (63) vs N = 62.
The unit of the LMM for S1-O1 is taken as one rating (rater random intercepts); the paper does not print the number of observations.
notes: Outcomes not listed as AI contrasts: CON vs HUM within BAS Drive groups (low Drive Δ = −0.35, p = 0.012, d = −0.64; high Drive p = 0.70; Fig. 3) compares two non-AI-partner conditions, though CON pools the GPT-4 seed set with two human seed sets. RMET correlated with within-subject range of originality (r = +0.27, p = .037, p. 5); random-forest variable importance of traits (Fig. 2, p. 5); self-reported outsourcing predicted lower originality with human partners (r = −0.504, p = .024, n = 20) and trended opposite with GPT-4 (β = +0.19), Δβ ≈ +0.35 (p. 5); perceived competence and responsiveness did not predict originality (BF01 = 16.40). These are moderator or trait analyses, not AI-vs-comparison contrasts. The 2-minute solo AUT (half before, half after the sessions) is described as a baseline and practice control; no results for it are reported. The paper says 'We release the platform, code, and dataset' (p. 1) but gives only the code repository and live-demo links (p. 2); data_url left empty. Randomization of solo-AUT timing is not stated.
